posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain point and add a sharper observation about explainability being the real missing layer in most BI tools
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes total sense. 'The model said so' isn't an audit trail — it's a liability. The funny thing is this problem isn't unique to ChatGPT, it's most analytics tooling. Numbers without a clear line back to source and logic have always been a compliance headache, AI just made it faster to create them. How are your teams handling the documentation side when a figure does get questioned?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption wall — validate that trust is the real product, not the dashboard
posts.draft_comment: 18 months on the build, then the real work starts. The thing nobody budgets for is the moment someone quotes a number from the dashboard in a board meeting and gets burned once — after that you're done, Excel wins forever. It's not a change management problem, it's a trust problem, and trust gets built one correct number at a time. How many of those finance team objections were actually about the tool vs. a bad number they saw early on?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add a layer about why that pattern keeps repeating, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That jump from 10% to 85% usage is the real metric most BI teams never track. The 47 KPIs thing isn't a data problem — it's a trust problem. When people don't trust that a number will hold up under scrutiny, they add more numbers to hide behind. Worth asking: what made those 5 stick when the other 42 didn't?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post that nails the governance failure of self-service BI — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and add the insight that the problem isn't access, it's accountability
posts.draft_comment: Three definitions of revenue is basically a rite of passage at this point. The license rollout feels like progress but you've really just distributed the chaos — now it lives in 200 places instead of one. The 'democratising data' story skipped over the bit where someone still has to decide what the numbers actually mean, and that someone needs real authority, not just a dashboard. Who in your org ended up being that person — or did no one?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare system reframing AI hallucinations as a security risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust/auditability layer that most analytics tools skip entirely
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right — hallucinated outputs aren't a UX problem, they're an integrity problem. Most analytics tools have invested heavily in access controls and data governance, then shipped an AI layer with basically zero auditability on what it generated or why. You'd never accept 'the model seemed confident' as a defence in a security audit. Why are we accepting it in a financial report?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with post validating BI tool failure in SMBs — reinforce the 'built for data teams not business teams' truth with a specific observation, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The £200k isn't even the real cost — it's the 18 months of 'we just need to get more people trained on it' before anyone admits it's not working. Most BI tools are designed to impress in a demo, not to answer the question a COO has at 8am on a Monday. The self-service promise always assumes the business user thinks like the person who built it. They never do.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market manufacturer hits a classic data trust problem — validate the culture diagnosis, add the layer that culture alone isn't enough without shared definitions baked into the tool itself
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is almost never about discipline — it's about three people who each had a perfectly logical reason for the filter they chose. Culture helps, but someone still has to decide which version of 'revenue' is the official one and make it impossible to accidentally use the wrong one. The CFO doesn't care who was right. They just stopped trusting the dashboard. How long does it usually take to win that trust back once it's gone?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem — validate that framing and reframe it as a data literacy gap, not a tool gap
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me — but I'd argue the problem isn't that people don't know what to ask, it's that they don't know what's even possible to ask. Shadow AI is the tell. When people go off-grid to get answers, it usually means the official tool made them feel dumb for trying. What would it change if the tool met users where they were instead of waiting for them to become power users?
